                                                  Abstract
     The aim of boosting is to convert a sequence of weak learners into a strong learner. At
     their heart, these methods are fully sequential. In this paper, we investigate the possibility
     of parallelizing boosting. Our main contribution is a strong negative result, implying
     that significant parallelization of boosting requires an exponential blow-up in the total
     computing resources needed for training.
     Keywords: Boosting, Generalization, Weak-to-Strong Learning, Parallelization


1. Introduction
Boosting is one of the most successful ideas in machine learning, allowing one to ”boost”
the performance of a base learning algorithm with rather poor accuracy into a highly ac-
curate classifier, with recent applications in adversarial training (Abernethy et al., 2021),
reinforcement learning (Brukhim et al., 2021), and federated learning (Hamer et al., 2020;
Shen et al., 2022), among many others. The classic boosting algorithm, known as Ad-
aBoost (Freund and Schapire, 1997), achieves this by iteratively training classifers on the
training data set. After each iteration, the data set is reweighed and a new classifier is
trained using a weighted loss function. The weights intuitively guide the attention of the
base learning algorithm towards training samples that the previous classifiers struggle with.
After a sufficiently large number of iterations, the produced classifiers are combined by
taking a weighted majority vote among their predictions.
    Both the classic AdaBoost algorithm, as well as more modern gradient boosters (Fried-
man, 2001; Ke et al., 2017; Chen and Guestrin, 2016), all have this highly sequential be-
haviour, where the algorithm runs in multiple iterations that adjust the learning problem
based on previously trained classifiers/regressors. Indeed, the best performance of gradient
boosters on benchmark data sets is often obtained after hundreds, or even thousands of
iterations (Natekin and Knoll, 2013). This may be appropriate when the base learning al-
gorithm has a small training time. However, it prevents the use of boosting in combination
with e.g. medium-sized neural networks as the base learning algorithm, or if one wishes to
use all available training data in a large data set. Here the sequential nature of boosting
algorithms is particularly critical, as it is not possible to simply distribute the training task
to many machines. This shortcoming of boosting algorithms was also highlighted in the
survey by Natekin and Knoll (2013) when discussing drawbacks of gradient boosting.
    In light of the above concerns, it would have a huge practical impact if a highly parallel
boosting algorithm could have been developed. Unfortunately, our main result shows that
parallelizing boosting cannot be done without an exponential increase in the total work
needed for training!

Weak to Strong Learning. To formalize the above claim that boosting cannot be paral-
lelized, we need to introduce the theoretical framework in which we prove our impossibility
result.
     Boosting was introduced to address a theoretical question by Kearns (1988); Kearns and
Valiant (1994), asking whether a so-called weak learner can always be converted to a strong
learner. In the following, we define these notions formally. First, let X be an input domain
and c : X → {−1, 1} an unknown concept that we want to learn.
     A γ-weak learner for a concept c : X → {−1, 1}, is an algorithm that given some constant
number of samples m0 labeled by c from any unknown distribution D over X , with constant
probability returns a hypothesis h : X → {−1, 1} such that LD (h) := Prx∼D [h(x) ̸= c(x)] ≤
1/2 − γ. It thus has an accuracy that is γ better than guessing. We say that the weak
learner has a γ advantage. We remark that whether or not the number of samples m0 is
allowed to depend on γ is irrelevant for our results and they apply in all circumstances.
     A strong learner on the other hand, is a learning algorithm such that for any 0 < ε, δ < 1,
there is some number of samples m(ε, δ), such that when given m(ε, δ) samples labeled by
c from any unknown distribution D over X , with probability at least 1 − δ, it returns
a hypothesis h : X → {−1, 1} such that LD (h) ≤ ε. A strong learner can thus obtain
arbitrarily high accuracy when given enough training data. We refer to m(ε, δ) as the
sample complexity of the strong learner.
     Kearns and Valiant thus asked whether the rather poor accuracy of a weak learner can
always be exploited to obtain a classifier with arbitrarily high accuracy, i.e. a strong learner.
This question was answered affirmatively by Schapire (1990), and AdaBoost is one example
of such a weak-to-strong learning algorithm. Concretely, the tightest known bounds on the
sample complexity of AdaBoost states that the hypothesis h it produces on a training set
S ∼ Dm of m samples, when using a γ-weak learner W as the base learning algorithm,
satisfies

    In weak-to-strong learning algorithms A, such as AdaBoost, a γ-weak learner W is
typically used by feeding it a distribution D over the training data S (e.g. the weighing over
the data set in each iteration of AdaBoost). It is then assumed that W returns a hypothesis
h with error at most 1/2 − γ under D. Note that this seems quite different from the above
definition of a γ-weak learner, where the weak learner receives at least m0 samples from
an unknown distribution D. However, the definition of a γ-weak learner actually implies
that W can compute a hypothesis h with error at most 1/2 − γ for a query distribution D
specified by A. This is because W is given access to the training data S and the distribution
D and thus it can just repeatedly sample m0 samples from D, compute a hypothesis from the

samples, and compute its exact error probability under D. If the error probability exceeds
1/2 − γ, W can just repeat with a fresh sample. Since W is a weak learner, this terminates
in an expected constant number of tries. Here one critically exploits that a weak learner
has advantage γ under any distribution when given at least m0 samples. Henceforth, we
thus think of a weak learner W as a procedure that we can query with a training set S, the
labels c(S) and a distribution D over S. It then returns a hypothesis h with LD ≤ 1/2 − γ.
A weak-to-strong learning algorithm A is then given query access to a γ-weak learner as
well as the training set S and the labels c(S). After querying W sufficiently many times to
obtain hypotheses h1 , . . . , hk , it must output a hypothesis h : X → {−1, 1}. Note that we
make no assumption that the output h is a voting classifier.

Parallel Weak to Strong Learning. We are now ready to define what we formally
mean by parallelizing boosting. We say that a weak-to-strong learning algorithm A has
parallel complexity (p, t) if it only invokes its weak learner W in p rounds. In each round,
it may query the weak learner with up to t different distributions D1 , . . . , Dt . The weak
learner then returns a hypothesis hi for each Di such that LDi (hi ) ≤ 1/2 − γ. The queries
made in any round may only depend on S, c(S) as well as the hypotheses obtained from W
in previous rounds. We let AS,c(S),W denote the hypothesis A reports on input S, c(S), W
when the p rounds are over.
    In this terminology, it is known that AdaBoost needs Θ(γ −2 ln m) iterations to obtain
the accuracy claimed in (1). It thus has parallel complexity (Θ(γ −2 ln m), 1). With parallel
complexity defined, we are finally ready to present our main result, ruling out parallel
boosting

Theorem 1 There is a universal constant a > 0 such that for any weak-to-strong learner
A, any m, any 0 < γ < a and any VC-dimension d, there exists a domain X , a concept
c : X → {−1, 1} and a γ-weak learner W for c, such that W uses a hypothesis set of
VC-dimension d and either: p ≥ exp(Ω(d)) or t ≥ min{exp(Ω(d/γ 2 )), exp(exp(Ω(d)))} or
LD (AS,c(S),W ) ≥ exp(−O(p max{γ, ln(tp)γ 2 /d})) in expectation over S and any random
choices of A. Here X , c and W depends on m, γ and d.

Let us discuss the implications of the theorem in detail. First, let us consider the simplest
case where one wants only a constant number of parallel rounds p = O(1). Then the lower
bound states that either t ≥ exp(Ω(d/γ 2 )), t ≥ exp(exp(Ω(d))) or the error probability
is at least exp(−O(max{γ, ln(t)γ 2 /d})). To make this error probability comparable to
AdaBoost (1) requires t = exp(Ω(dγ −2 ln m)). Thus there is no way around either an
exponential dependency on dγ −2 or a double-exponential dependency on d.
    If one is willing to use a super-constant number of rounds p, then there are a couple
of possibilities for obtaining an error probability comparable to (1). First, one could have
either p = exp(Ω(d)), t = exp(Ω(dγ −2 )) or t = exp(exp(Ω(d))). These bounds are all
exponential in either the VC-dimension or γ −2 or both. Finally, there is the possibility of
making the error e−O(pγ) small. To make it comparable to (1) requires p = Ω(γ −1 ln m).
This is only a γ factor less than AdaBoost. Thus there is unfortunately not much hope
for parallelizing boosting, and certainly not to a near-constant number of rounds. In all
circumstances, if the number of rounds is significantly less than γ −1 ln m, then it requires
an exponential number of queries t per round.

Previous Lower Bounds for Parallelizing Boosting. Let us conclude by discussing
related work by Long and Servedio (2013). In their work, they also study the parallel com-
plexity of boosting, however under somewhat different assumptions. Concretely, they prove
a lower bound showing that any weak-to-strong learner must have parallel complexity (p, t)
satisfying p = Ω(γ −2 ln m), regardless of the number of calls per round t. This strength-
ens a previous result by Freund (1995) and is quantitatively a stronger lower bound than
ours. However, they also model the problem in a way that makes their result weaker than
ours. First, they make no assumption on the complexity/VC-dimension of the hypothesis
set used by the weak-learner. On close inspection of their construction, their input domain
X is the full cube {−1, 1}k with k = Θ(γ −2 ln m) and they have one hypothesis hi for each
coordinate i, making the prediction hi (x) = xi . The VC-dimension of this hypothesis set is
⌊lg2 k⌋ = Θ(ln(1/γ) + ln ln m), i.e. growing with m.
    Secondly, and just as crucially, their lower bound assumes that the query distribu-
tions fed to the weak learner are obtained by ”filtering”. Concretely, this means that the

tor of predictions made by previously obtained hypotheses on x as well as the label c(x) (see

using the bounded VC-dimension to define these distributions, thereby circumventing their
lower bound.


2. Impossibility of Parallelization
In this section, we prove our main result, Theorem 1, stating that boosting can not be
parallelized significantly without a major reduction in accuracy. We start by presenting the
basic setup for our proof, then the high level ideas leading to the lower bound, followed by
the formal details.

Basic Setup. Let A be an arbitrary, possibly randomized, weak-to-strong learning al-
gorithm with parallel complexity (p, t). For any d, m and γ, we aim to design a γ-weak
learner W for a concept c : X → {−1, 1}, using a hypothesis set H of VC-dimension d,
such that A run with W as its weak learner must have a generalization error at least that
stated in Theorem 1. We use the simple input domain X = {x1 , . . . , x2m } and the hard
data distribution D is the uniform distribution over X .
    Observe that if p ≥ exp(Ω(d)), t ≥ exp(Ω(d/γ 2 )) or t ≥ exp(exp(Ω(d))), we have nothing

Hard Concept Distribution. We next describe our hard distribution over a concept c
and corresponding γ-weak learner W. The distribution over c is simply the uniform distri-
bution, i.e. every x ∈ X is mapped independently to either −1 or 1 with equal probability.
This is a natural hard distribution, as under this distribution, the training data S, c(S) only
provides information about labels of points in the training data.
    Now observe that our data distribution is uniform over X = {x1 , . . . , x2m } and S ∼ Dm
consists of m samples. Thus there are at least m samples that are not part of the training
data. Without querying the weak learner W, an algorithm A has no knowledge of these
labels and can at best try to guess them with success probability 1/2, leading to a constant
error probability as a fresh sample x ∼ D falls outside the training data with probability at
least 1/2.

Hard Weak Learner Distribution. In light of the above, we aim to design a γ-weak
learner W such that its replies reveal as little as possible information about the labels
outside the training data.
    For this, we conceptually think of its hypothesis set H as consisting of p groups H1 , . . . , Hp .
For each of these groups, starting with H1 , we have a random subset Xi of X . We let X1
be a uniform random 2m/β sized subset of X and let Xi be a uniform random 2mβ −i sized
subset of Xi−1 for a parameter β > 1 to be determined. We then form Hi by drawing 2d/2
random hypotheses as follows: For each hypothesis h ∈ Hi , we let h(x) = c(x) for x ∈         / Xi
and we let h(x) be uniform random and independently chosen for x ∈ Xi . We then add
another 2d/2 random hypotheses to Hi . These are simply chosen such that they return a
uniform random label on every element x ∈ X . Finally, we also add c to the hypothesis
set H. Since we assume p ≤ exp(ad) for a sufficiently small constant a, we have that the
hypothesis set has at most 2d hypotheses and thus has VC-dimension at most d.
    The weak learner W does the following upon being queried for a distribution D′ over
X : It searches through the hypothesis sets Hi , starting with i = 1, and returns the first
hypothesis h it sees with LD′ (h) ≤ 1/2 − γ. If no such h exists in any Hi , it simply returns
c.

Intuition. Let us discuss the main ideas in the design of the above (random) weak learner
W. We think of the hypothesis sets Hi and corresponding subsets Xi as being responsible
for one parallel round each, where H1 , X1 is responsible for the first round.
    If we consider the very first round, then observe that X1 is a random β −1 -fraction of X .
Since this subset is unknown to a deterministic A, if it queries W with a distribution D′
that is somewhat uniform over X , then about a 1 − β −1 fraction of the mass is on points
x ∈ X with x ∈      / X1 . Each of the first 2d/2 hypotheses h in H1 has h(x) = c(x) on such
points, and thus immediately have an expected advantage of 1 − β −1 . If 1 − β −1 ≈ γ, then
there is an overwhelming probability that W can answer all queries made in the first round
using hypotheses from H1 .
    Now assume that after i rounds, it holds that W has only returned hypotheses from
H1 , . . . , Hi . Then for round i + 1, even if A learns all hypotheses in H1 , . . . , Hi , the subset
Xi+1 is again an unknown β −1 -fraction of Xi . It follows that the weak learner can again
answer any queries made by A using only Hi+1 . Continuing this argument implies that
after all p rounds have been completed, the weak learner W never returned the hypothesis
c. Now even if A sees all of H1 , . . . , Hp , it still has no knowledge of the labels assigned by c

3. Single-Round Boosting
In this section, we demonstrate a single-round parallel boosting algorithm with good gen-
eralization performance. Our algorithm initially asks a number of queries in parallel to a
γ-weak learner. Following that, it has several sequential rounds in which it decides how
to combine the obtained hypotheses. We comment that this is a single-round algorithm
according to our definition of parallel complexity. Moreover, invoking the weak learner ef-
fectively corresponds to training a model, whereas the later sequential steps of our algorithm
use only inference. In practical setups where training is significantly more expensive than
inference, this may still be a major speed up. Furthermore, our algorithm demonstrates the
near-tightness of our lower bound.
    The goal of our algorithm is to produce a voting classifier with large margins on all
training samples. Concretely, given a γ-weak learner W and m samples                m

is to produce a voting classifier f (x) = sign(g(x)) with g(x) = (1/k) i=1 hi (x) such that
for every training sample (x, c(x)) ∈ S, it holds that c(x)g(x) ≥ γ/16. Generalization of
this voting classifier then follows from generalization bounds for voting classifiers with large
margins, see e.g. Breiman (1999); Gao and Zhou (2013); Bartlett et al. (1998). We note
that we assume that the weak learner W always returns a hypothesis with error at most
1/2 − γ under the distribution D it is queried with.

4. Conclusion
In this work, we established strong barriers for the possibilities of parallelizing boosting.
Concretely, to parallelize below O(γ −1 ln m) rounds incurs an exponential blow-up in the
number of invocations of a weak learner.
    The classic algorithms, such as AdaBoost, use O(γ −2 ln m) rounds. Thus it is conceivable
that boosting can be somewhat parallelized. We leave this as an exciting direction for future
research.
    We also complemented our lower bound by a near-optimal single-round boosting al-
gorithm. A slightly unsatisfactory aspect of our single-round algorithm is that performs
sequential work in O(γ −2 ln m) rounds after having invoked the weak learner/trained a
number of hypotheses. It would be interesting to obtain a truly parallel algorithm also
when accounting for post-processing of trained models.
